title: Data centre boom drive structural LNG demand in Southeast Asia
gist: Wood Mackenzie finds hyperscale data centre growth is creating a structural, credit-backed LNG demand base in Southeast Asia (16% annual LNG demand growth through 2035, led by Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand), while India's cheaper renewables-plus-storage economics and gas infrastructure gaps keep LNG structurally locked out of the region's much larger data centre buildout.

themes.theme: Southeast Asia's structural LNG demand signal

insights.claim: Southeast Asia's data centre power pipeline is set to more than triple from 2.8 GW today to 9.4 GW by 2035, with data centre electricity demand growing from 17 TWh to 57 TWh over the same period.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sizes the underlying power-demand base that LNG suppliers and gas-fired power developers are underwriting new capacity against.
insights.quote: Southeast Asia’s data centre pipeline is set to more than triple from 2.8 gigawatts (GW) today to 9.4 GW by 2035, with electricity demand from data centres growing from 17 terawatt-hours (TWh) to 57 TWh over the same period.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts Southeast Asia LNG demand will grow 16% annually through 2035 on the back of hyperscale data centre expansion, in direct contrast to South Asia where a renewables-dominated grid shuts gas out entirely.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gives investors a quantified, region-specific bull case for SE Asia LNG offtake growth to size against upcoming project FIDs and regas capacity additions.
insights.quote: Hyperscale expansion drives 16% annual LNG demand growth in Southeast Asia through 2035, while India’s renewables-dominated grid shuts gas out entirely

insights.claim: Combined-cycle gas turbines are currently the only technology able to meet data centres' 24/7 reliability requirements at scale in Southeast Asia because grid-scale battery storage will remain commercially immature across the region through the mid-2030s.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Identifies battery-cost/maturity timing as the single assumption underpinning the LNG demand thesis; faster-than-expected battery cost declines would be the key risk to monitor against this call.

insights.claim: Data centre operators are a new class of LNG counterparty because they are large, creditworthy off-takers whose power demand stays stable through economic cycles, which changes the risk calculus for financing new LNG supply into Southeast Asia.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Improved counterparty credit quality can lower the risk premium on new LNG supply contracts and regas/import infrastructure financing in the region.
insights.quote: These are large, creditworthy off-takers with power needs that remain stable regardless of economic cycles.
insights.locator: Omarali quote, para after SE Asia overview

insights.claim: Singapore's grid runs on approximately 95% gas today, so virtually every new data centre megawatt translates almost directly into incremental LNG offtake, and with piped imports from Malaysia and Indonesia expected to cease by the early 2030s, Singapore's LNG reliance is on course to reach 100%.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Singapore becomes a near pure-play, near-total LNG demand market as piped gas disappears — a clean proxy for regional LNG price sensitivity to data centre growth.
insights.quote: Singapore’s grid runs on approximately 95% gas today, meaning virtually every new data centre megawatt translates almost directly into incremental LNG offtake.

insights.claim: Malaysia and Thailand offer the biggest LNG growth opportunity in the region because both are seeing steady declines in domestic and piped gas supply, making LNG the only fuel option to support new gas-fired power plants.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Declining domestic production forces incremental power growth onto imported LNG, making these two markets the highest-conviction near-term LNG demand adds in the region.

insights.claim: Malaysia has 3.9 GW of data centre capacity under development, and new LNG regasification terminals are being built specifically to meet the resulting growth in power demand.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Concrete pipeline capacity to track for regas terminal FIDs, capex commitments and LNG import contract awards in Malaysia.

insights.claim: In Thailand, where two-thirds of the grid is already gas-fired, LNG's share of gas supply is expected to exceed 50% by 2035 as Gulf of Thailand production and Myanmar pipeline imports continue to decline.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A crossover point (LNG >50% of gas supply) that marks Thailand's shift from a piped-gas market to an LNG-import-dependent one, relevant for terminal capacity planning and offtake contracting.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Omarali frames Malaysia and Thailand as being at a turning point where data centre investment is accelerating just as domestic gas output peaks and declines, with new import infrastructure and a broadening importer base making current timing important for LNG suppliers with volumes to place.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Explicit timing call: LNG suppliers with uncommitted volumes have a near-term window to contract into a broadening Malaysia/Thailand importer base before the market matures.
insights.quote: Malaysia and Thailand are at a turning point. Data centre investment is growing quickly just as domestic gas output peaks and declines.
insights.locator: Omarali quote, end of Malaysia/Thailand section

insights.claim: Indonesia's Batam is emerging as the third node of the Singapore-Johor-Riau (SIJORI) corridor, with over 450 MW of data centre capacity in the pipeline and strong policy support, but power deliverability and grid reliability remain the binding constraint on capturing this demand.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Flags grid reliability, not policy or capital, as the actual gating factor for Batam's data centre and associated LNG demand growth — a variable to track separately from headline capacity announcements.

insights.claim: India's data centre market is set to grow fivefold to nearly 12 GW by 2035, making it the second-largest market in Asia Pacific and attracting an estimated US$145 billion of investment between 2024 and 2030.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: India's data centre buildout is nearly as large as Southeast Asia's in absolute power terms but represents essentially zero incremental LNG demand — a key divergence for anyone modeling Asian LNG demand off aggregate data centre capacity.
insights.quote: India’s data centre market is set to grow fivefold to nearly 12 GW by 2035, making it the second largest in Asia Pacific and attracting an estimated US$145 billion in investment between 2024 and 2030.

insights.claim: LNG-to-power generation costs two to three times more than renewables paired with battery storage in India, making gas economically unviable as a baseload fuel for data centres there.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A direct cost mechanism explaining why India diverges from Southeast Asia: unlike SE Asia, India's renewables-plus-storage economics already beat gas, removing the CCGT bridge argument entirely.
insights.quote: LNG-to-power generation costs two to three times more than renewables paired with battery storage in India, making gas economically unviable as a baseload fuel for data centres.

insights.claim: Gas currently accounts for under 2% of India's power generation mix and is forecast to remain at that level through the outlook period, as coal and renewables continue to dominate.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A structural, not cyclical, ceiling on Indian gas demand — rules out a "catch-up" LNG demand story for India even as its data centre capacity scales toward SE Asia's.

insights.claim: Pipeline infrastructure gaps across key data centre corridors in southern, central and eastern India add a further barrier to gas penetration beyond the cost disadvantage.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Even a favorable cost shift for gas would still face a multi-year physical infrastructure buildout in these corridors, extending any realistic timeline for Indian gas-fired data centre power.

insights.claim: None of India's hyperscalers have announced gas-backed power supply agreements, while the commercial and industrial renewable power purchase agreement market has already exceeded 33 GW of contracted data centre capacity.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Revealed preference from actual contracting activity confirms the cost/infrastructure thesis: hyperscalers are voting with capital for renewables over gas in India, a signal LNG-exposed investors should treat as near-term confirmation, not just a forecast.
insights.quote: None of India’s hyperscalers have announced gas-backed power supply agreements, with the commercial and industrial renewable power purchase agreement market having already exceeded 33 GW of contracted data centre capacity.

insights.claim: Pakistan and Bangladesh face persistent load-shedding, grid instability and macroeconomic pressures that limit data centre demand and deter hyperscale investment, compounding South Asia's structural exclusion from the LNG-for-data-centres story.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Even if India's cost dynamics shifted, neighboring South Asian markets have independent macro and grid barriers, reinforcing that South Asia is not a near-term LNG demand region on any timeline.
